text:
Where to go next

Lakens (2022), Improving Your Statistical Inferences (free online), especially the chapters on p values, likelihoods, and Bayesian statistics, which walk through common misconceptions about Bayes factors.
Kristoffer Magnusson’s interactive visualizations: Bayesian inference and confidence intervals.
Bayes Rules! (Johnson, Ott, & Dogucu, 2022), free at bayesrulesbook.com, for a full course in applied Bayesian modeling in R.
bayesEd (Papenberg), an R package that visualizes the Bayesian t-test as a prediction contest; Scene 2 follows the same logic.
Informative hypotheses such as “enjoyment: rewarded > no consequence > punished” can be tested directly with Bayes factors (Hoijtink et al., 2019; R package bain).
In communication: Konijn et al. (2015) reanalyze media-violence and mediated-communication datasets with Bayes factors and argue this can reduce publication bias. Levine et al. (2008) critique NHST practice in quantitative communication research.

title: Scene 6 · What each framework promises
text:
Frequentist methods make promises about procedures: if you follow the plan, you will wrongly claim an effect in at most α of the studies where none exists. Bayesian methods make statements about this dataset under this model and prior. Here is what happens when researchers peek at their data every 10 participants per group and stop when they like the result. R/simulate_data.R ran 2,000 studies per scenario (a minute or two); we load the summary.






Explainer: false positives, power, peeking






False-positive rate: among studies where the true effect is zero, the share that claim an effect. With p < .05 and one planned analysis, it is 5%.
Power: among studies where the effect is real, the share that detect it (here, reach p < .05).
Peeking (optional stopping): checking results repeatedly as data come in and stopping once they look good. Each extra look is another chance for noise to cross the threshold.
Sequential design: a plan that builds in repeated looks, with thresholds chosen in advance so error rates stay controlled.

Figure 1: Left: when there is no effect, how often each rule claims one (dashed lines: one look at n per group; solid: peeking every 10 per group). Right: when the true effect is small (δ = 0.30), how often a single look at n per group gives each result.











How to read this figure




Left: studies where there is no true effect. The vertical axis is the share that claimed one; the horizontal axis is how many participants per group had been collected.
Dashed lines: one planned analysis at that sample size. Solid lines: peeking every 10 participants per group and stopping at the first “success.”
Right: studies of a real but small effect (δ = 0.30), each analyzed once at the given sample size. Gray is power; blue is the share with at least moderate evidence for the effect; orange is the share with moderate evidence against it, which is misleading here.




Peeking breaks the p value’s promise. With one look, false positives stay at 5%. Peeking every 10 participants inflates them to about 20%.
Bayes factors are not immune either. BF₁₀ > 3 is a stricter criterion than p < .05 at these sample sizes, so it starts with fewer false alarms (about 1.5% with one look at 100 per group). Peeking still multiplies them, here to about 8%. The Bayes factor still means what it says about the data in hand (Rouder, 2014), but if you act on a threshold, you need to know how often that action misleads, and the guarantees depend on the prior (de Heide & Grünwald, 2021).
Sequential designs have to be planned. Sequential Bayes factor designs set their thresholds and minimum sample size by simulation to keep misleading evidence rare (Schönbrodt et al., 2017). With lax settings (stop at BF 3 or 1/3, first look at 10 per group), 56% of simulated studies of a real δ = 0.30 effect stop with “evidence for no effect.”
Default Bayes factors can mislead toward the null when true effects are small. At 50 per group, 32% of studies of a real δ = 0.30 effect produce “moderate evidence” for no effect, because the default alternative expected bigger effects. This is Scene 2’s lesson again: the prior is part of the hypothesis.

Theory-building takeaway. If your field needs claims that are rarely wrong in the long run, frequentist error control is the tool. If it needs graded evidence among specific theories, Bayes factors are. Either way, plan the analysis before seeing the data.

Explainer: vote counting, fixed-effect meta-analysis, sequential updating






Vote counting: tallying how many studies were significant. It ignores effect sizes and precision, and with modest power it will often report “mixed results” for a real effect.
Fixed-effect meta-analysis: a weighted average of the study estimates, with weights of 1 / SE², so more precise studies count more. It assumes every lab estimates the same true effect. When labs’ true effects differ, a random-effects model estimates that variation too.
Sequential updating: with normal approximations, each lab’s posterior (a mean and an SD) becomes the prior for the next lab.




Counting significant results (“vote counting”) says 2 of 6. Combining the evidence says something else. Two ways to combine:

Fixed-effect meta-analysis (frequentist): weight each lab by 1 / SE² and average.
Sequential Bayesian updating: start from a prior, update with lab 1, and let yesterday’s posterior be today’s prior (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018) for lab 2, and so on.


cumulate <- function(prior_mean, prior_sd) {
  m <- prior_mean; s <- prior_sd; out <- NULL
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(lab_stats))) {
    u <- update_normal(m, s, lab_stats$diff[k], lab_stats$se[k]); m <- u[["mean"]]; s <- u[["sd"]]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(after_lab = k, mean = m, lo = m - 1.96 * s, hi = m + 1.96 * s,
                                 p_pos = pnorm(0, m, s, lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out
}
fe <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(lab_stats)), function(k) {
  w <- 1 / lab_stats$se[1:k]^2; m <- sum(w * lab_stats$diff[1:k]) / sum(w); se <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))
  data.frame(after_lab = k, mean = m, lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(m / se)))
}))
vague <- cumulate(0, 10)
skept <- cumulate(0, 0.25)

Right: the combined estimate after each lab, from a fixed-effect meta-analysis and from sequential Bayesian updating with a vague or skeptical prior.











How to read this figure




Left (a forest plot): each row is one lab’s estimated difference with its 95% CI. Filled dots reached p < .05; open dots did not. The black diamond is the pooled estimate from all six labs.
Most of the open-dot intervals include the pooled estimate: a nonsignificant lab is not evidence against the effect.
Right: the combined estimate as labs are added one at a time (1 = lab 1 alone; 6 = all six). Each color is one way of combining; the bars are 95% intervals. The dashed line is the true effect built into the simulation.
The gray (meta-analysis) and blue (vague-prior Bayes) results are the same numbers. The orange (skeptical-prior) results start lower and move toward them as data accumulate.

With a vague prior, sequential Bayesian updating reproduces the fixed-effect meta-analysis to the third decimal. The skeptical prior starts lower and moves toward the others as labs accumulate: the prior’s weight shrinks as data grow (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018, Example 4).






What each framework lets you say




Frequentist: “Pooling six labs, enjoyment was 0.38 points higher after the rewarded ending, 95% CI [0.19, 0.57].”
Bayesian: “After six labs, even a skeptic’s posterior probability that the effect is positive exceeds 99.9%.”
Neither: “Only two of six labs replicated the effect.” That sentence confuses the significance of each study with the evidence of all of them.



Theory-building takeaway. Theories are built across studies, not within one. Bayesian updating makes accumulation explicit, and meta-analysis does the same job with long-run guarantees. If labs differ in their true effects (the “for whom and where” question), the natural next step is a hierarchical model that estimates the variation itself.






Your turn




Drop lab 6 (the “failed” replication). How much does the pooled estimate move? What would a literature that only published labs 2 and 5 conclude?
Use lab 1’s posterior as the prior for Study 1’s n = 150 data. Is that legitimate here? What would make it illegitimate?

title: Scene 2 · Priors as theories
text:
So far ADT has made one directional prediction: more enjoyment after the rewarded ending. Theory building usually means weighing rival explanations of the same result, so here are two rivals. To compare the three, each account now states how big δ should be. All three are stylized (simplified for this demo, not summaries of a literature):
A theory that predicts “δ is around 0.3” can be written as a prior on δ. That prior implies which t statistics the study should produce. The Bayes factor is the ratio of how well two hypotheses predicted the t value we actually observed (Rouder et al., 2009; Gronau et al., 2020). Treating priors as part of the theory is the core of Vanpaemel’s (2010) defense of Bayes factors for theory testing.
Load the Study 1 data
s1_50  <- read.csv("data/story_n50.csv")
s1_150 <- read.csv("data/story_n150.csv")
s50  <- two_group(s1_50)

  "Craft (δ = 0)" = "null",
  "ADT: Normal(0.3, 0.15)" = prior_adt,
  "Tragedy: Normal(−0.3, 0.15)" = prior_tragedy,
  "JASP default: Cauchy(0, 0.707)" = prior_default
)

text:
How much does the prior width matter?
This recreates JASP’s robustness check: the default hypothesis with Cauchy widths from 0.05 to 1.5.


Code
r <- seq(0.05, 1.5, by = 0.025)
rob <- rbind(data.frame(r, bf = sapply(r, function(w) bf_vs_null(s50,  function(x) dcauchy(x, 0, w))), n = "n = 50 per group"),
             data.frame(r, bf = sapply(r, function(w) bf_vs_null(s150, function(x) dcauchy(x, 0, w))), n = "n = 150 per group"))

  geom_vline(xintercept = sqrt(2) / 2, color = pal[["gray"]], linetype = "dotted") +

  annotate("text", x = 0.72, y = 150, label = "JASP default (0.707)", hjust = 0, size = 4, color = pal[["ink2"]]) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100), limits = c(0.3, 200)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("n = 50 per group" = pal[["blue"]], "n = 150 per group" = pal[["aqua"]])) +
  labs(x = "Cauchy prior width r", y = "BF10 (log scale)") +
  theme_demo()








Figure 2: Bayes factor for a Cauchy alternative as its width changes. Wider priors predict larger effects and are penalized when the observed effect is small.











How to read this figure




Horizontal axis: the width (scale) of the default Cauchy prior. Small widths say “expect small effects”; large widths say “expect large ones.”
Vertical axis: BF₁₀ on a log scale. The solid line at 1 means no preference; the dashed lines at 3 and 10 mark JASP’s “moderate” and “strong” labels.
The dotted vertical line is JASP’s default width (0.707).
A flat curve means the conclusion does not depend on the prior’s width; a sloped curve means it does.



At n = 50 every width gives weak evidence at best, and wide priors tip toward the null. At n = 150 every reasonable width favors an effect. A prior sensitivity analysis is how you show readers which conclusions depend on your theory’s specifics and which do not.

title: Scene 2 · Priors as theories
section: The frequentist counterpart: test the theory’s value, not only zero
text:
The frequentist counterpart: test the theory’s value, not only zero
A p value can test any hypothesized value, not only zero (Greenland et al., 2016). Testing each account’s central prediction:

p_delta <- function(s, d0) { # exact test of H0: delta = d0 via the noncentral t
  lo <- pt(s$t, s$df, ncp = d0 * sqrt(s$neff)); 2 * min(lo, 1 - lo)
}
sapply(c(`Tragedy (delta = -0.3)` = -0.3, `Craft (delta = 0)` = 0, `ADT (delta = 0.3)` = 0.3),
       function(d0) c(`n = 50` = p_delta(s50, d0), `n = 150` = p_delta(s150, d0))) |> round(3)

        Tragedy (delta = -0.3) Craft (delta = 0) ADT (delta = 0.3)
n = 50                   0.001             0.054             0.660
n = 150                  0.000             0.000             0.316


At n = 50 the data reject the tragedy account’s value but cannot separate zero from 0.3. At n = 150 zero is rejected and 0.3 is not. The frequentist route falsifies values that are incompatible with the data; it does not quantify how much the data support one surviving value over another. For range predictions (“at least 0.2”), use minimum-effect and equivalence tests (Lakens et al., 2018; Scene 3).






What each framework lets you say




Frequentist: “The data are incompatible with the tragedy account’s effect of −0.3 (p < .001) and compatible with both zero and 0.3 (n = 50).”
Bayesian: “The data were about 5 times more likely under the ADT account than under no effect, and 8 times more likely under no effect than under the tragedy account.”



Theory-building takeaway. A Bayes factor is only as meaningful as the hypotheses it compares. Default priors test a default theory. To test your theory, write its prediction down as a prior, and report how conclusions change across defensible alternatives.






Your turn




Make the ADT prior more confident: Normal(0.3, 0.05). Does its Bayes factor go up or down at n = 50? Why?
Write a prior for a “large effect” account, Normal(0.8, 0.2). How does it fare at n = 150, where the observed d is 0.42?

title: One Story, Two Inference Machines
text:
The running example
A class example from earlier in the semester, made concrete. Participants read a short story in which the main character does a good deed: they find a lost wallet and return it to its owner with the cash untouched. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two endings. In the rewarded ending, the grateful owner gives the character a cash reward. In the punished ending, the owner accuses the character of stealing from the wallet and calls the police. Everyone then rates how much they enjoyed the story, from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much). The good deed is identical in both versions; only its consequence differs.
Affective disposition theory (ADT) says what should happen (Raney, 2004). Viewers judge what characters do, come to like characters who do good, and want those characters to fare well. Enjoyment depends on whether they do: it rises when a liked character is rewarded and falls when a liked character is punished. Returning a wallet full of cash makes the character easy to like, so ADT predicts:








Ending
What happens
ADT predicts




Good + Rewarded
The character returns the wallet and gets a cash reward.
higher enjoyment


Good + Punished
The character returns the wallet and is accused of stealing.
lower enjoyment



We summarize the effect as a standardized difference, δ = (rewarded − punished) / SD, so ADT predicts δ > 0. Scene 2 adds two rival accounts that predict something else.






Explainer: what is δ?



δ (Greek delta) is the true standardized effect: the difference between the two conditions’ population means, divided by the standard deviation within each condition.
δ = (true mean, rewarded − true mean, punished) ÷ within-group SD

The Greek letter marks an unknown population value. Its estimate from a sample is Cohen’s d; in the n = 50 study, d = 0.39.
Standardizing puts effects measured on different scales on one ruler. It is also the scale on which JASP’s Bayesian t-test, and this notebook, places priors.
In these data the SD is about 1.2 scale points, so δ = 0.30 means enjoyment ratings about 0.36 points higher on the 1–7 scale. Put another way, the average participant in the rewarded condition would report more enjoyment than about 62% of participants in the punished condition.
Cohen’s rough labels (0.2 “small,” 0.5 “medium,” 0.8 “large”) are common, but they are no substitute for deciding what size of effect matters for your question. Scene 3 returns to this.



Keep the course’s chain in view: Explanation → Prediction → Design & data generation → Analysis → Inference. Today lives in the last two links, but Scene 5 shows why the middle link decides what the last one can mean.

The data
All files are in data/. R/simulate_data.R documents every data-generating process and rebuilds Studies 2–4; the three Study 1 files were generated earlier from the same process and are kept verbatim so the numbers match the course notes. As with most classroom examples, random seeds were chosen so each dataset illustrates its point cleanly. Change a seed and rerun to see how much a single study bounces around.

The frequentist question: how surprising are these data if the model were true?

t.test(enjoyment ~ factor(condition, levels = c("rewarded", "punished")),
       data = s1_50, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  enjoyment by factor(condition, levels = c("rewarded", "punished"))
t = 1.9496, df = 98, p-value = 0.05408

 -0.007504973  0.847504973

mean in group rewarded mean in group punished 
                  4.54                   4.12 


The difference is 0.42 points, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.85], p = .054. The p value is the probability of a t statistic at least this far from zero if every assumption of the model held, including a true difference of exactly zero (Greenland et al., 2016). It is not the probability that the null is true.






Explainer: the t statistic





The t statistic is the observed difference divided by its standard error: how many standard errors the difference sits away from zero. Here, 0.42 ÷ 0.215 ≈ 1.95. If the true difference were zero (and the model’s other assumptions held), t values at least this far from zero, in either direction, would occur about 5.4% of the time. That share is the p value.

title: Scene 1 · Same data, two questions
section: From one p value to a p-value function
text:
From one p value to a p-value function
A p value tests one hypothesized value, usually zero. Nothing stops us from testing other values. Here are ordinary t-tests of the same n = 50 data against five different hypothesized true differences:

rewarded <- s1_50$enjoyment[s1_50$condition == "rewarded"]
punished <- s1_50$enjoyment[s1_50$condition == "punished"]
mu0 <- c(0, 0.2, 0.42, 0.6, 0.85)
p_at_mu0 <- sapply(mu0, function(m) t.test(rewarded, punished, mu = m, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value)
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Null hypothesis: true difference =` = mu0, `Two-sided p` = sprintf("%.3f", p_at_mu0),
                        check.names = FALSE), align = "cc")

Each row is the same test you already know; only the null value changes. The p value is 1 when the hypothesized difference equals the observed one (0.42) and shrinks as the hypothesis moves away from it in either direction. Do this for every possible value, connect the results, and you get the p-value function, also called a compatibility curve: how compatible the data are with each possible true difference (Greenland et al., 2016). The 95% CI is simply the set of values where the curve sits above .05. The figure adds the curve for the n = 150 study for comparison.

mu <- sort(c(seq(-0.6, 1.4, by = 0.005), s50$diff, s150$diff))  # include each exact peak

Figure 1: The p-value function for Study 1 at two sample sizes. Each point on a curve is a t-test of that study’s data against one hypothesized true difference, so each curve peaks (p = 1) at its own study’s observed difference. Thick segments at p = .05 mark the 95% CIs.











How to read this figure




Horizontal axis: candidate values for the true difference, in scale points. Each one is a possible null hypothesis.
Vertical axis: the two-sided p value from testing the data against that candidate. The five dots on the blue curve are the five tests in the table above.
The peak of each curve (the dot at p = 1) sits at that study’s observed difference: no candidate is more compatible with the data. The two peaks differ because each curve comes from its own dataset, with its own estimate (0.42 points at n = 50, 0.47 at n = 150). Both estimates scatter around the same true effect. A bigger study gives a narrower curve, but its estimate is not guaranteed to land closer to the truth.
The usual reported p value is the height of the curve at zero (p = .054 for n = 50).
Where the curve crosses the dashed p = .05 line are the limits of the 95% CI (the thick segments).
A narrower curve means a more precise estimate. With n = 150 (aqua), fewer values remain compatible, and zero is no longer among them.
Caution: the height is not the probability that a value is true. It says how surprising the data would be if that value were true.



At n = 50, zero is barely inside the compatible range, and so are differences as large as 0.85 points. “No effect” and “a fairly large effect” are both compatible with these data.

title: Scene 1 · Same data, two questions
section: The Bayesian question: given these data, what should I believe about the difference?
text:
The Bayesian question: given these data, what should I believe about the difference?
Bayesian estimation starts from a prior (what you believed before), multiplies it by the likelihood (how well each candidate value predicts the data), and normalizes to get the posterior (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018). We do it the most transparent way possible: evaluate prior × likelihood at a fine grid of candidate values (every 0.0025 points from −3 to 4) and rescale so the area is 1. This is called grid approximation.






Explainer: prior, likelihood, posterior






Prior: a probability distribution over the possible true differences before seeing these data. “Normal(0, 0.25)” means centered on 0 with SD 0.25, so about 95% of the prior’s weight sits between −0.5 and +0.5.
Likelihood: for each candidate true difference, how probable the observed data would be if that candidate were true. It is not a probability distribution over the candidates; it scores how well each one predicted the data.
Posterior: prior × likelihood, rescaled so the total area is 1. It is the updated distribution over the true difference after seeing the data.
Grid approximation: instead of solving the math, compute prior × likelihood at thousands of closely spaced candidate values and add them up. It works whenever there are only one or two unknowns (Johnson et al., 2022, ch. 6).




We compare two priors on the raw difference:

Flat: every difference equally plausible beforehand.
Skeptical: Normal(0, 0.25). Most effects of message features on enjoyment are small; 95% of the prior sits within ±0.5 points.

flat      <- grid_posterior(grid, rep(1, length(grid)),  lik_diff(s50, grid))
skeptical <- grid_posterior(grid, dnorm(grid, 0, 0.25),  lik_diff(s50, grid))

rbind(flat = post_summary(grid, flat$posterior),
      skeptical = post_summary(grid, skeptical$posterior)) |> round(3)

        data.frame(x = g$x, y = g$posterior,  what = "posterior",  panel = label))

Figure 2: Prior (gray, dashed), likelihood (orange), and posterior (blue) for the n = 50 data. The flat prior’s posterior is the likelihood itself.











How to read this figure




Each panel starts from a different prior (gray, dashed): flat on the left, skeptical on the right.
The likelihood (orange) is the same in both panels, because the data do not change with the prior. On the left it is hidden under the posterior.
The posterior (blue) combines the two. With a flat prior it coincides with the likelihood; with the skeptical prior it sits between prior and likelihood, pulled toward zero and narrower than either.
The area under the blue curve to the right of the vertical line at zero is P(difference > 0).



Two things to notice:

With a flat prior, the 95% credible interval equals the 95% confidence interval to the second decimal. The numbers are identical; the sentences are not. The credible interval licenses “there is a 95% probability the difference lies in this range, given the model and prior.” The CI does not.
The flat prior gives P(difference > 0) = 0.973, which is 1 minus the one-sided p value (0.027). Same arithmetic, different question answered. The skeptical prior pulls the estimate toward zero and makes you less sure of the sign.







Explainer: confidence interval vs. credible interval (CrI)






A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that, over many repetitions of the study, captures the true value 95% of the time. Any single interval either contains the true value or does not; the 95% describes the procedure, not this interval (Greenland et al., 2016).
A 95% credible interval (CrI) contains 95% of the posterior distribution. Given the model and the prior, there is a 95% probability that the true value lies inside this interval.
With a flat prior the two can be numerically identical, as here. They still license different sentences.

section: The Bayes factor: a third question
text:
The Bayes factor: a third question

bf50 <- bf_default(s1_50)   # JASP default: Cauchy prior on δ with scale 0.707
bf50

Bayes factor analysis
--------------
[1] Alt., r=0.707 : 1.123621 ±0.01%

Against denominator:
  Null, mu1-mu2 = 0 
---
Bayes factor type: BFindepSample, JZS


The posterior said “probably positive,” yet BF₁₀ ≈ 1.12 says the data barely distinguish “no effect” from the default alternative. Both are Bayesian. They disagree because they answer different questions:

Estimation assumes there is some difference and asks how big it is.
The Bayes factor compares two models: one where the difference is exactly zero, and one where it is spread out according to a prior (here the JASP default, a Cauchy with scale 0.707 on δ). It asks which model predicted the observed data better. Scene 2 opens that box.







Explainer: reading a Bayes factor






BF₁₀ is how probable the observed data are under H₁ (an effect, with its possible sizes described by a prior) divided by how probable they are under H₀ (no effect). The subscripts say which hypothesis is on top: BF₁₀ = 3 means the data were three times more likely under H₁. BF₀₁ = 1 / BF₁₀ flips it.
Near 1, the data do not discriminate between the two hypotheses. JASP prints verbal labels: 1–3 “anecdotal,” 3–10 “moderate,” 10–30 “strong,” 30–100 “very strong,” above 100 “extreme.” These are conventions, not thresholds.
A Bayes factor is not the probability that H₁ is true. Getting there requires prior odds: posterior odds = prior odds × Bayes factor (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018).
JASP’s default H₁ puts a Cauchy prior on δ with scale 0.707: a bell-shaped curve centered at zero with heavy tails. Half its weight lies between δ = −0.707 and +0.707, so it expects moderate-to-large effects and allows very large ones.

The same true effect (δ = 0.30) generated all three rows; by design, only the sample size differs. The estimates still bounce around from row to row (sampling variability), but precision improves steadily: the intervals narrow as n grows. The skeptical prior also matters less and less as the data overwhelm it.






What each framework lets you say (n = 50)




Frequentist: “Enjoyment was 0.42 points higher after the rewarded ending, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.85], p = .054. The data are compatible with differences from about zero to 0.85 points.”
Bayesian estimation: “Under a flat prior, there is a 97% posterior probability that the true mean difference is positive; under a skeptical prior, 93%.”
Bayes factor: “The data are about equally likely under no effect and under the default alternative (BF₁₀ = 1.12).” That is a statement about these two hypotheses only; Scene 2 shows a sharper alternative doing better.



Theory-building takeaway. A p value and a posterior are answers to different questions. Decide which question your theory needs answered before you look at the output.






Your turn

title: Scene 3 · When a theory predicts nothing
text:
ADT says endings matter because viewers like the character. So the effect should disappear when viewers have no reason to like the character: if the character does something morally neutral instead of returning the wallet (say, they buy a coffee), viewers form no disposition toward them, and a reward or punishment at the end should leave enjoyment unchanged. A rival “happy ending” account (people enjoy stories that end well, whoever the character is) predicts the effect survives. Study 2 is the boundary test. A theory that says where an effect should not appear is a stronger theory, but only if you can support a null.
neutral <- read.csv("data/story_neutral_n200.csv")
# "pilot" = the interim look: the first 40 participants per group of the same study
pilot <- rbind(head(neutral[neutral$condition == "rewarded", ], 40),
               head(neutral[neutral$condition == "punished", ], 40))
sl_p <- two_group(pilot); sl_f <- two_group(neutral)

title: Scene 3 · When a theory predicts nothing
section: Frequentist: a nonsignificant result is not evidence of absence, but an equivalence test can be
text:
Frequentist: a nonsignificant result is not evidence of absence, but an equivalence test can be
First we decide what “no effect” means: the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). Here we stipulate ±0.3 scale points (about δ = 0.25), smaller than the effect in Study 1. That choice deserves argument; the analysis is only as good as it is. Then the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure asks whether the difference is significantly above −0.3 and significantly below +0.3 (Lakens et al., 2018). Equivalently: is the 90% CI inside the bounds?

sesoi <- 0.3
rbind(
  interim = c(diff = sl_p$diff, p_nhst = sl_p$p, p_tost = tost(sl_p, sesoi)$p_tost),
  full  = c(diff = sl_f$diff, p_nhst = sl_f$p, p_tost = tost(sl_f, sesoi)$p_tost)

section: Bayesian: evidence for the null, and posterior mass inside the “no effect” region
text:
Bayesian: evidence for the null, and posterior mass inside the “no effect” region
The Bayes factor can favor the null directly: BF₀₁ = 1 / BF₁₀. And the posterior on δ tells us how much probability sits inside a region of practical equivalence (ROPE), here δ within ±0.25, matching the SESOI (Kruschke & Liddell, 2018).

rope <- c(-sesoi, sesoi) / 1.2        # ±0.3 points on a scale with SD ≈ 1.2
prior_happy <- prior_adt   # the happy-ending account predicts Study 1's effect survives: Normal(0.3, 0.15)
bayes_null <- function(s) {
  post <- delta_posterior(s, prior_default)
  c(BF01_vs_default = 1 / bf_vs_null(s, prior_default),
    BF01_vs_happy = 1 / bf_vs_null(s, prior_happy),
    P_in_ROPE = unname(post_summary(post$x, post$posterior, rope = rope)["p_rope"]))
}

Figure 1: Left: difference estimates with 90% (thick) and 95% (thin) CIs against the ±0.3-point equivalence bounds. Right: posterior for δ under the default prior, with the ROPE shaded.











How to read this figure




Left: each row is one look at the data. The dot is the observed difference; the thick blue bar is the 90% CI and the thin line the 95% CI. The shaded band marks the ±0.3-point equivalence bounds.
Equivalence is established when the thick 90% bar lies entirely inside the band. At 40 per group it sticks out; at 200 per group it fits.
Right: the posterior for δ (under the default prior) at each look. The shaded band is the ROPE (±0.25 in δ units, the same ±0.3 points). The more of a curve’s area inside the band, the stronger the case that the effect is practically zero.



At the interim look, p = .283 says nothing about absence: the TOST fails (p = .415). The default Bayes factor leans toward the null (2.6 to 1), but against the rival that matters, the happy-ending account, the interim data slightly favor it (BF₀₁ = 0.69). Which alternative you test changes the verdict. At 200 per group, both frameworks support the boundary claim: the TOST rejects true differences of ±0.3 points or larger (p = .011), and the data favor the null by about 9 to 1 over the default alternative and 5.6 to 1 over the happy-ending account.






What each framework lets you say (full study)




Frequentist: “We can reject true differences of ±0.3 points or larger (TOST p = .011), so the effect, if any, is smaller than our smallest effect of interest.”
Bayesian: “The data were 9 times more likely under no effect than under the default alternative, and 5.6 times more likely than under the happy-ending account; 99% of the posterior lies within ±0.25 SD.”
Both require that you said in advance what counts as “no effect” (a SESOI or a prior). Neither lets you conclude absence from p > .05 alone (Dienes, 2014; Lakens et al., 2020).



Theory-building takeaway. Boundary conditions are how theories become specific. Supporting “the effect vanishes for a morally neutral character” separates ADT from a happy-ending account, but only a design powered for equivalence can deliver that.






Your turn




Shrink the SESOI to ±0.1 points. What sample size would the TOST need?
At the interim look, BF₀₁ was about 2.6 against the default alternative but below 1 against the happy-ending account. Why does the default alternative lose to the null so easily? (Hint: look at what the Cauchy prior predicts in Scene 2.)

title: Scene 5 · Neither machine fixes the design
text:
Every result in the earlier scenes came from a randomized experiment. A coin flip decided who read the rewarded ending and who read the punished one, so the two groups differed, on average, only in the ending. That is why those scenes could argue about how much evidence there was and how to phrase it, but never about what caused the difference. The design, not the analysis, is what licensed reading the difference as an effect of the ending.
Much of communication research cannot randomize. People choose what they watch, read, and share, and those choices are often exactly what we want to study. This scene asks what happens to both inference machines when the design no longer does the causal work. The short answer is in the title. A p value, a posterior, and a Bayes factor all summarize what the data say about an association; none of them can say whether that association is the causal effect.
In the course’s chain (Explanation → Prediction → Design & data generation → Analysis → Inference), the earlier scenes worked in the last two links. This scene steps back to the middle link and shows why it decides what the last one can mean.

title: Scene 5 · Neither machine fixes the design
section: Study 4: the same question, but viewers choose
text:
Study 4: the same question, but viewers choose
Study 4 asks Study 1’s question with data a streaming platform already collects. The platform offers two versions of the same episode: one where the character’s good deed is rewarded (the rewarded episode) and one where it is punished. Viewers choose which version to watch, and afterward they rate how much they enjoyed it.
The choice is the problem. Some viewers have a stable preference for stories where good is rewarded (call it just-world preference). They are more likely to pick the rewarded episode, and they tend to enjoy stories more whichever version they watch. So the ending and the preference arrive together, and comparing the two groups of viewers mixes the effect of the ending with the effect of who chose it.
One more piece matters for deciding what to control for. The ending affects enjoyment partly through satisfaction with the ending (did the character get what they deserved?). That path is part of the effect we want to estimate, not a nuisance to remove.






Predict first



The platform has 600 viewers, twice as many as Study 1’s largest sample (300). Will its estimate be closer to the truth than the experiment’s? Which variables would you control for?

title: Scene 5 · Neither machine fixes the design
text:
Drawing the design
Rohrer (2018) offers a tool for reasoning about this before touching the data: draw a causal diagram (a DAG) of what causes what, then read off which variables to adjust for and which to leave alone. The diagram is a theory of the design, stated clearly enough that readers can dispute it.






Explainer: DAG vocabulary (Rohrer, 2018)






DAG (directed acyclic graph): a diagram of assumed causal relationships. Arrows point from cause to effect, and no path loops back on itself.
Confounder: a common cause of the exposure and the outcome (here, just-world preference). It creates a non-causal association, a back-door path, that has to be blocked, for example by adjusting for the confounder.
Mediator: a variable on the causal path from exposure to outcome (here, satisfaction with the ending). Adjusting for it removes part of the effect you are trying to estimate.
Collider: a variable caused by two others. Adjusting for it, or selecting on it, creates a spurious association. Your turn question 1 explores this.
Estimand: the quantity you are trying to estimate. The total effect includes every path from exposure to outcome; the direct effect excludes the path through the mediator.






Code
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, title) {
  e <- merge(merge(edges, nodes, by.x = "from", by.y = "id"), nodes, by.x = "to", by.y = "id", suffixes = c("", "_to"))
  shrink <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, a = 0.17, b = 0.19) {
    dx <- x1 - x0; dy <- y1 - y0; L <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
    data.frame(sx = x0 + dx * a / L, sy = y0 + dy * a / L, ex = x1 - dx * b / L, ey = y1 - dy * b / L)
  }
  seg <- cbind(e, shrink(e$x, e$y, e$x_to, e$y_to))
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x = sx, y = sy, xend = ex, yend = ey, color = type), linewidth = 1.1,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4.2, label.size = 0.3,
               label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines"), fill = "#fcfcfb", color = pal[["ink"]]) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(causal = pal[["blue"]], confound = pal[["orange"]], other = pal[["gray"]])) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.35, 1.35), ylim = c(-0.8, 1.25)) +
    labs(title = title) + theme_void(base_size = 15) +
    theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
          plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fcfcfb", color = NA))
}

How to read this figure




Boxes are variables; arrows are causal effects.
Blue arrows are the effect we want: the episode’s effect on enjoyment, both directly and through satisfaction with the ending.
Orange arrows form the back-door path: just-world preference influences both which episode people choose and how much they enjoy it.
In the experiment, a coin flip decides the episode, so no arrow points from just-world preference into it and the back door is closed.

title: Scene 5 · Neither machine fixes the design
section: Three analyses of the platform data
text:
Three analyses of the platform data
Now analyze the platform data three ways, changing only what the model controls for: nothing (the naive comparison), the confounder (just-world preference), or the confounder plus the mediator (satisfaction with the ending). Each model gets both treatments: a frequentist estimate with its 95% CI and p value, and Bayesian posteriors (flat and skeptical priors) with a Bayes factor. Because the data are simulated, we know the right answer, and the figure below marks it.

obs <- read.csv("data/story_observational.csv")
models <- list(
  "Naive: no controls"                   = enjoyment ~ chose_rewarded,
  "Adjust for just-world preference"     = enjoyment ~ chose_rewarded + just_world,
  "Also adjust for satisfaction (mediator)" = enjoyment ~ chose_rewarded + just_world + satisfaction
)
fit_both <- function(f) {
  m <- lm(f, data = obs)
  est <- coef(m)[["chose_rewarded"]]; se <- sqrt(vcov(m)["chose_rewarded", "chose_rewarded"])
  df <- m$df.residual; ci <- est + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, df) * se
  # Bayesian: flat prior -> posterior is a t centered on the OLS estimate
  # Skeptical prior Normal(0, 0.25) on the coefficient (normal approximation)
  sk <- update_normal(0, 0.25, est, se)
  # Bayes factor for including chose_rewarded, holding the other predictors.
  # lmBF treats the 0/1 predictor as continuous with its default prior scale
  # (sqrt(2)/4), a different default from the t-tests in Scenes 1-3.
  full <- lmBF(f, data = obs)
  rest <- all.vars(f)[-(1:2)]
  bf <- if (length(rest) == 0) extractBF(full)$bf else
    extractBF(full / lmBF(reformulate(rest, "enjoyment"), data = obs))$bf
  data.frame(est = est, lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], p = 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df),
             P_pos_flat = pt(est / se, df), sk_mean = sk[["mean"]],
             sk_lo = sk[["mean"]] - 1.96 * sk[["sd"]], sk_hi = sk[["mean"]] + 1.96 * sk[["sd"]], bf10 = bf)
}

Figure 2: Estimates of the rewarded-episode effect under three adjustment sets. Black: 95% CI, identical to the flat-prior credible interval. Blue: posterior under a skeptical prior. Dashed lines: the true total and direct effects built into the simulation. Gray: the randomized Study 1 estimate (n = 150).











How to read this figure




Each row is one analysis of the rewarded-episode effect. The top (gray) row is the randomized experiment, for reference.
Black dots and bars are the estimate and its 95% CI, which here equals the flat-prior credible interval. Blue dots and bars are the posterior under a skeptical prior.
The dashed lines mark the truth built into the simulation: the total effect (aqua, 0.36) and the direct effect (gray, 0.16).
An interval that is narrow but far from the dashed line is precise and still wrong about the causal effect. That is the naive row.



Read the naive row carefully. With 600 viewers, every framework is confident about the wrong quantity: p < .001, an enormous Bayes factor, a narrow credible interval, and an estimate more than double the causal effect. The association is real; reading it as the causal effect is the error. A skeptical prior barely dents it. Adjusting for the confounder recovers the total effect. Adding the mediator “controls away” part of the effect you wanted and leaves only the direct path; that is a different estimand, not a more careful estimate of the same one (Rohrer, 2018; Wysocki et al., 2022).






What each framework lets you say




Both frameworks, naive model: “Viewers who chose the rewarded episode enjoyed it 0.89 points more.” True as a description. As a causal claim, it assumes no common causes of choice and enjoyment, and the measured just-world variable already shows that assumption is false.
After adjustment: “Assuming just-world preference is the only common cause, choosing the rewarded episode raised enjoyment by 0.34 points.” The assumption is now in the sentence, where readers can dispute it.



Theory-building takeaway. A p value, a Bayes factor, and a posterior all describe what the data say about a coefficient. The design and the causal diagram decide which coefficient is the causal effect. Inference frameworks operate downstream of identification.
